Lymphedema

Randomized trials suggest PBM can reduce short-term arm swelling in breast-cancer-related lymphedema, with possible gains in grip strength and pain. A small head-and-neck pilot also found improvement, while longer-term effects and results for other sites remain less certain.

Summary of the Evidence

Recent randomized evidence suggests that PBM can reduce swelling in breast-cancer-related upper-limb lymphedema, with possible improvement in grip strength and pain. A 2026 meta-analysis rated these outcomes moderate certainty, but a 2025 review reached different conclusions for swelling and grip strength. A small head-and-neck trial adds a separate preliminary signal for external edema and function. Durability and effects in other forms of lymphedema remain uncertain.

Human and clinical evidence

Qian et al. included nine randomized trials with 312 participants with breast-cancer-related lymphedema. Pooled results favored PBM for arm volume, circumference, grip strength, and pain. The review rated certainty moderate, with low-to-moderate heterogeneity and stable sensitivity analyses. Swelling outcomes were not evident at about two weeks, became more favorable around four weeks, and remained favorable at eight weeks. The twelve-week subgroup was not statistically significant and included fewer studies and participants. Adverse events were reported sparsely, leaving safety less certain than symptom and function outcomes (Qian et al. 2026).

An earlier review by Hussein et al. searched through August 2023 and included 11 randomized trials with 379 participants, pooling eight. Its meta-analysis found no significant pooled effect on arm circumference, volume, grip strength, or quality of life, while pain and some shoulder-mobility measures favored PBM. The included trial set and pooled comparisons differed from those in the newer review, so the two syntheses do not yet give a consistent estimate for every outcome (Hussein et al. 2025).

Chiu et al. reported that swelling outcomes were more favorable in regimen subgroups using three sessions per week at 1.5–2 J/cm² and treatment courses longer than 15 sessions. These subgroup patterns are informative about studied schedules but do not establish an optimal protocol (Chiu et al. 2023).

A 2026 pilot randomized wait-list trial enrolled 25 head-and-neck cancer survivors after standard decongestive therapy. At eight weeks, external lymphedema severity, symptom burden, and neck range of motion favored PBM. The study was small and unblinded, did not assess internal edema, and did not establish longer-term durability (Deng et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

One mouse-tail study reported reduced tail thickness at selected time points, alongside lower inflammatory changes and greater lymphatic-vessel growth after laser treatment. This supports a possible biological mechanism but does not establish clinical benefit (Jang et al. 2016).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Breast-cancer trials mainly used red or near-infrared lasers directed at the axillary lymphatics or affected arm, alongside or compared with usual lymphedema care. Treatment lasted about three to twelve weeks, with schedules ranging from daily exposure to twice weekly and variable fluence and treatment area. Chiu et al. found more favorable swelling results in some higher-frequency and longer-course subgroups, but the evidence does not establish one optimal regimen.

The head-and-neck pilot used a 904-nm superpulsed laser at 1.5 J/cm². It treated 12–21 face and neck points for 60 seconds each, twice weekly for six weeks, after brief manual lymphatic drainage. Some database records concern far-infrared devices, which do not all represent the same light source or treatment approach.

Interpretation

For breast-cancer-related upper-limb lymphedema, recent pooled results are favorable, but an earlier synthesis found no pooled improvement for swelling or grip strength. Small trial sets, differing eligibility and outcomes, short follow-up, and sparse safety reporting leave uncertainty. Evidence for external head-and-neck outcomes is preliminary, and evidence for internal edema or durable benefit is very limited. PBM is best considered a possible adjunct to established lymphedema care.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Breast-cancer-related arm swelling — limb volume favored PBM (SMD −0.78, 95% CI −1.03 to −0.54) and circumference was 3.61 cm lower on average (95% CI 2.38–4.85 cm lower). The newer review rated certainty moderate (Qian et al. 2026).

Grip strength and pain — grip strength was 1.72 kg higher (95% CI 1.07–2.37 kg); pain intensity favored PBM by 0.29 points on the review’s pooled measure (95% CI 0.05–0.52 points lower; Qian et al. 2026).

Earlier synthesis — Hussein et al. found no significant pooled difference in arm circumference immediately after treatment or at three months, and no significant grip-strength difference. Pain favored PBM but was highly heterogeneous; some shoulder-mobility measures also favored PBM (Hussein et al. 2025).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Moderate for short-term arm swelling, grip strength, and pain in breast-cancer-related upper-limb lymphedema.

Low for short-term external head-and-neck outcomes.

Very low for durable effects beyond short follow-up or internal head-and-neck edema.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

A 2026 review of nine randomized trials rated evidence moderate for arm volume, circumference, grip strength, and pain. A 2025 review with a different set of 11 trials found no pooled benefit for swelling or grip strength, although pain and some shoulder measures favored PBM. Small samples, short follow-up, differing pooled results, and sparse safety reporting limit confidence. Head-and-neck evidence comes from one small, unblinded pilot.
